title: Relief Ratio Calculator: Terrain Steepness Index
description: Calculate a basin's relief ratio with the Relief Ratio Calculator — relief divided by length, the geomorphologist's steepness index. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a drainage basin dropping 850 m over its 12.4 km length has a relief ratio of 0.0685 — equivalent to an average slope of about 3.9 degrees from rim to mouth.
quick_answer: The Relief Ratio Calculator computes the relief ratio of a basin or slope — its total elevation drop divided by its horizontal length. Enter the relief and the length and read the ratio: the compact steepness index geomorphologists use to compare basins, predict sediment behaviour and characterise terrain.

body.t: Relief ratio tracks how energetically a basin can move sediment — steeper ratios mean faster water and coarser loads. Basin heights come from the
'Mountainous' versus 'rolling' becomes a number two field crews can share — Appalachian basins versus Alpine ones stop being adjectives.
A corridor's relief ratio previews its grading burden before anyone profiles it in detail — the screening number that decides which valleys get the survey.
Schumm's relief ratio (1956) is a first-week computation in drainage-basin analysis — this page is the worked-example machine for it.
Gentle basin: 300 m of relief over 20 km → 0.015 (a lazy 0.86° average). Mountain basin: 1,500 m over 8 km → 0.1875 (10.6°). Same formula, landscapes an order of magnitude apart in behaviour.

examples.label: Example · Reading the ratio as a slope

body.t: The ratio is the tangent of the average slope angle: 0.0685 ↔ 3.92°, 0.1875 ↔ 10.62°. Converting ratio to degrees is how field intuition checks the spreadsheet.

rows: Extreme relief — young, steep, fast-eroding terrain
popular_table.note: Definition: maximum basin relief (highest minus lowest elevation) divided by the basin's longest horizontal dimension parallel to the main drainage. State your length convention when publishing — ratios compare only like with like.

faq: Closely related but not identical: the ratio uses the basin's total relief and longest dimension, while average slope averages local gradients. Two basins can share a ratio with very different internal slopes.
The standard (Schumm) uses the maximum basin length parallel to the principal drainage line. The longest-dimension convention is what makes published ratios comparable.
Unitless — metres over metres or feet over feet, the ratio cancels. Mixed units are the one way to break it, so convert first (the elevation converters on this site oblige).
A cousin index: relief divided by the square root of basin area. Relief ratio is the older, length-based measure; ruggedness suits fan and debris-flow screening better.
For whole basins, practically never; for a single slope face or a short gully reach, yes — cliffs are locally ratio-rich, which is why the index is defined at basin scale.
